measure.title: Point at the Sun, and you point at a place on Earth
measure.mini: The compass bearing you turn to when you face the Sun is the bearing of one particular place: the place with the Sun straight overhead at that instant. That holds whatever the Sun's distance.
measure.text: Two numbers are measured when you face a body in the sky: its bearing from true north, the azimuth, and its height above the horizontal, the altitude. This argument uses only the bearing, which is cheap to measure: a stick, its shadow, and a way of finding true north. The claim is not that the Sun is far or near, large or small. It is that the bearing you turn to when you face the Sun is the bearing of a particular place on Earth, the place that has the Sun straight overhead at that instant, whatever the Sun's distance turns out to be. The drawing is schematic.
measure.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Sun bearings that do not point along the great circle toward the place with the Sun overhead.
subpoint.title: The place with the Sun overhead
subpoint.mini: At every instant there is one place on Earth with the Sun straight overhead: the subsolar point. The Sun, that point and the Earth's centre lie on one line.
subpoint.text: At every instant there is exactly one place on Earth where a body stands straight overhead, its sub-body point: for the Sun, the subsolar point. By definition, the body, that point and the Earth's centre lie on one straight line. It moves west at 15° of longitude per hour and north and south with the seasons, and nautical almanacs tabulate it hour by hour. The same holds for the Moon and every star. The drawing is schematic.
subpoint.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a Sun whose bearing from many places does not converge on one point on the ground.
bearing.title: The azimuth is the bearing to the subsolar point
bearing.mini: The Sun's azimuth, measured from true north, is exactly the starting bearing of the great circle to the subsolar point. Not approximately, and with no dependence on the Sun's distance.
bearing.text: The azimuth of any body, measured from true north, is exactly the initial great-circle bearing to its sub-body point, with no dependence on the body's distance. Two lines of proof: the sub-body point, the Earth's centre and the body lie on one line; the observer's vertical also passes through the centre. So the vertical plane containing the observer and the body contains the centre, therefore the whole line from centre to body, therefore the sub-body point. Same vertical plane, same azimuth. The Sun at 150 million km and the Moon at 384,000 km obey the same rule, and so would a lamp at 5,000 km. Every value can be checked against the U.S. Naval Observatory [1]. The drawing is schematic.
bearing.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: measured azimuths that differ from the great-circle bearing to the subsolar point.
aedisc.title: Bearings on the flat-earth map
aedisc.mini: On the polar flat-earth map, radius stands for colatitude and angle for longitude. On it, the Sun should be seen along the straight line toward the point beneath it, with north meaning the centre of the map.
aedisc.text: The flat-earth map is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection: the North Pole at the centre, each place at a radius equal to its colatitude, at an angle equal to its longitude [1]. If the Earth were this map, the Sun, standing over its subsolar point, would be seen from anywhere along the straight line toward that point, and north would be the direction of the map's centre. That gives each observer a definite bearing to compare with the one measured. A different projection would give different bearings, but one that repaired the bearings would have to break the distances instead. The drawing is schematic.
aedisc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Sun bearings matching the straight lines on this map, everywhere.
globe.title: Seven observatories, one Sun: the globe
globe.mini: Seven real seismic stations around the world, one instant. On the globe the Sun's rays arrive parallel; each station's bearing is the direction of its own vertical plane through them. All seven meet at the subsolar point.
globe.text: Seven places, the real stations of the Global Seismographic Network [1], and one instant, named above the text. The globe is seen from the side with the Sun's rays drawn: they are parallel because they are computed from the Sun's real distance. At exactly one point the ray runs straight down a radius: the subsolar point. Each coloured arc is where a station's vertical plane meets the ground, and its bearing is the one every station would measure. Every value can be checked against the U.S. Naval Observatory [2] or NOAA's solar calculator [3]. A side view shows only the near face, so a station round the edge may be hidden.
globe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the seven stations' measured Sun bearings disagreeing with the globe's by more than a degree.
flat.title: Seven observatories, one Sun: the flat map
flat.mini: The same instant on the flat-earth map. Each station's Sun bearing is drawn as a half-line, using the map's own north. On a correct map they would all run into the Sun. They do not, and far south they point almost the opposite way.
flat.text: The same instant, named above the text, on the north-polar azimuthal equidistant map [1], in the orientation flat maps are always printed. From each station, a half-line leaves at the bearing measured there, which anyone can check against the U.S. Naval Observatory [2], using the map's own definition of north, the direction of its centre. On a correct map all the half-lines would run into the Sun's position. In the far north they nearly do; the map is least wrong near its centre. Further south the disagreement changes sign and passes 90°: at the December instant, a station on the Ross Ice Shelf is told to look almost due north for a Sun that is almost due south. Played through the day, the disagreement moves; it never resolves. The shaded triangle is where three of those half-lines, from the stations farthest apart, cross one another: on a correct map they would cross at a single point, the Sun's position, and its longest side, printed above, measures the error.
flat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: bearings measured at southern stations that converge on the Sun's position on this map.
both.title: Where does each observatory look?
both.mini: Seven real observatories, one instant. On the globe, every measured Sun bearing leads to the one place with the Sun overhead. On the flat-earth map the same bearings scatter, and in the far south they point almost the opposite way.
both.text: Seven stations of the Global Seismographic Network [1] at the instant named above the text, under both models. On the globe the Sun's rays arrive parallel, and each station's bearing is the direction of its own vertical plane through them: every one leads to the subsolar point. On the flat-earth map [3], the same bearings, which anyone can check against the U.S. Naval Observatory [2], are drawn from each station using the map's own north; on a correct map they would all run into the Sun. They meet only near the map's centre. Further south they change sign, and at the December instant a station on the Ross Ice Shelf is told to look almost due north for a Sun almost due south. That is the difference between turning left and turning right. The shaded triangle is where three of the half-lines cross: on a correct map, a single point.
both.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern stations' measured bearings converging on the Sun's position on the flat map.
parallax.title: Parallax: the Earth's radius seen from the Moon
parallax.mini: Horizontal parallax is the angle the Earth's radius subtends at a body. For the Moon it reaches about a degree, twice its own width, and it moves the Moon along its vertical circle: the altitude changes, the bearing does not.
parallax.text: Horizontal parallax is the angle the Earth's radius subtends as seen from a body, with the right angle at the point of tangency. For the Moon it is close to a degree, twice its own diameter [1], so the Moon seen from the surface sits measurably lower than from the Earth's centre. The shift is along the vertical circle, from the zenith through the body: the altitude changes and the bearing does not, so it leaves the azimuth argument untouched. The altitude it shifts is the oldest measurement of the Moon's distance there is; Ptolemy measured it with an instrument built for the purpose [2]. For the Sun, across the whole planet, the shift is some sixteen arcseconds. The drawing is schematic.
parallax.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a Moon that stays above the horizon from every place at once, as a lamp over a plane must.
baseline.title: Two observers, one Moon, one distance
baseline.mini: Two observers a known baseline apart look at the Moon at the same instant. The small angle between their sight lines gives its distance. In 1751, Lalande in Berlin and Lacaille at the Cape did it on nearly the same meridian.
baseline.text: Two observers a known baseline apart see the Moon at the same instant in slightly different directions, and the opening between their sight lines gives its distance. The same two observations give two independent results: the bearing, from which distance vanishes, and the difference in altitude, which is nothing but the distance. In 1751 Lacaille observed the Moon from the Cape of Good Hope while the young Lalande observed it from Berlin, on very nearly the same meridian, ten thousand kilometres apart [1]. The method fails for the Sun, which shifts by only about sixteen arcseconds across the whole planet, and that failure shows the method is not manufacturing its answer. The drawing is schematic.
baseline.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a lunar parallax that fits a lamp at one height, the same from every pair of stations.
